chapters.title: First Tablet
paragraphs: Let the man who has tested the heart of every matter instruct the nation. Possessing knowledge of everything, he shall give all the people that teaching. He shall pass on his wisdom (?) so that together they may take part in it. Gilgamish (?) was the master of wisdom, knowing all things. He uncovered the hidden secret . . . Yes, he passed down the account of events before the Flood. He travelled far, utterly exhausted and worn out by his labour (?), and carved the whole record of his hardship on a stone tablet.

He raised the fortifications of high-walled Erech. It was he who secured, firm as brass, the foundations of sacred E-Anna, the holy treasury. He strengthened its base to allow no one passage . . . the threshold which from ancient times (?) . . . E-Anna . . . to let no one through (?) . . .
(About thirty lines are missing. The description of Gilgamish continues into the next column.)
He is divine in two parts out of three, and human in the remaining third . . . His body’s shape . . . He has compelled to take . . .
(Approximately three lines are missing here.)

“. . . of Erech he has taken . . . while his head rises like an aurochs’. No blow from a weapon equals his; his fellows are driven into the snares, while Erech’s warriors cower, un- . . . Gilgamish lets no father keep his son. His pride grows with every day and every night. Yes, he is the shepherd of high-walled Erech; he is our (?) shepherd . . . commanding, overbearing, cunning . . . Gilgamish lets no mother keep her girl, no warrior his daughter, and no husband his wife.”

The Immortals listened to the appeal of their cries. The heavenly gods spoke to Anu, the lord of Erech: “You have fathered a son who is altogether a tyrant, his head rearing like an aurochs’. No one can match the impact of his weapons. His fellows are driven into the snares, while Erech’s warriors cower, un- . . . Gilgamish allows no father to keep his son. Day after day, night after night, his arrogance increases. Yes, he is the shepherd of Erech with its high walls; he is their shepherd . . . domineering, powerful, crafty . . . Gilgamish leaves no girl with her mother, no daughter with a warrior, nor any wife with her husband.”

Anu heard the appeal of their lamentation and summoned the lady Aruru. “Aruru, you were the one who fashioned the first seed of humanity (?). Now fashion its counterpart, so that he may encounter Gilgamish, yes, on the day of his pleasure. Let the two contend against each other, and let him bring Erech some relief.”

On hearing this, the goddess Aruru immediately shaped Anu’s idea in her mind. She washed her hands, then worked some clay with her fingers and moulded it out in the desert. There she made Enkidu, a warrior, as though born and begotten, yes, a second Ninurta. Hair grew out over his whole body. He bound his locks in a band as a woman does. His hair sprang up thickly like the bristles of barley. He knew neither a people nor a country, and his clothing was like Sumuqan’s. He grazed on plants beside the gazelles, drank his fill alongside the cattle, and took pleasure in the water together with the beasts.

Then a hunter who set traps came face to face with him. He encountered him at the animals’ watering place on one day, then a second, then a third. At the sight of him, terror spread over the hunter’s face. He and his cattle returned to his homestead, alarmed and frightened. He cried out, his heart troubled and his expression dark . . . distress in his belly . . . Yes, his face looked like that of someone who had travelled a great distance.

The hunter began to speak to his father. “Father, an immense fellow has come out of the mountains. Oh, his strength surpasses everyone’s throughout the country. His enormous power makes him like another Anu himself. Always (?) he roams freely over the mountains; always he grazes with the cattle and makes his way to the water. I am afraid to go near him. He has filled in the pits I dug with my own hands and ripped up the traps I laid. He has helped all the cattle, the wild creatures of the desert, get away from my grasp. He will not let me practise my skills as a hunter.”

His father spoke in reply to the hunter. “My son, Gilgamish lives in Erech, and no one has ever defeated him. His strength is the greatest anywhere in the country. His vast power is like that of a second Anu himself. Go towards Erech. When he hears about this monster, he will say, ‘Hunter, go and take a courtesan, a hetaera, with you . . . like a strong one. When he brings the cattle together again at their watering place, let her remove her cloak and show her lovely beauty. He will see her, and surely he will hold her in his arms. From that moment the cattle reared in his own deserts will reject him.’”

The hunter listened to his father’s advice and at once set off for Gilgamish. He took the road to Erech, came before Gilgamish and addressed him: “An enormous fellow has emerged from the mountains. Oh, no one in the whole country can rival his strength. His tremendous power is like that of another Anu himself. Always (?) he wanders over the mountains at will, grazes on plants with the cattle, and goes to the water. I am afraid to approach him. He has filled back in the pits I dug with my own hands and torn up the traps I set. All the cattle, the creatures of the desert, he has helped escape from my clutches. He prevents me from carrying on my work as a hunter.”

Gilgamish gave the hunter this answer: “My good hunter, go and bring a courtesan, a hetaera, along with you. When he gathers the cattle at their watering place once more, she must take off her cloak and reveal her beautiful body. He will catch sight of her and surely take her in his arms. Then the cattle that grew up in his very own deserts will immediately refuse to have him among them.”

The hunter set out, taking a courtesan, a hetaera, along. Together they began their travels and went on their journey. After three days they reached the pleasant place they had chosen. The hunter and the hetaera sat down in hiding (?). For a day, then a second day, they waited beside the place where the animals drank. At last the cattle arrived and began drinking their fill.

The animals came there to enjoy the water. Enkidu was among them, the man born of the mountains. He grazed on plants with the gazelles and drank all he wanted with the cattle, taking pleasure in the water beside the other beasts. The courtesan saw him, that huge, vigorous fellow, a completely wild creature from the desert’s depths! “Girl, that is him! Uncover your beauty and show him how lovely you are, so he can possess you. Do not feel shy at all. Captivate his soul. As soon as he sees you he will certainly come towards you. Then loosen your cloak, let him embrace you, and use a woman’s arts on him. The animals born in his desert will immediately reject him, because he has held you against his chest.”

The girl bared her breasts and displayed her beauty so that he could possess her. She felt no shyness: she captivated his soul and loosened her cloak. He embraced her, and she used a woman’s arts as he held her against his breast. In this way Enkidu spent six days and seven nights lingering with the courtesan, making love to her.

At last satisfied with her charms, he turned towards his cattle. Oh, how the gazelles ran off the moment they noticed him! The desert animals fled from him, yes, from Enkidu! He had lost his innocence. As the cattle ran away, his knees gave out, and he could no longer run as swiftly as before. Yet through this he had reached his full maturity and gained a wider understanding.

He sat down once more at the woman’s feet. She studied his face, and he listened to what she said. “Enkidu, you are handsome; you shall be just like a god. Why do you keep wandering through the desert with the wild animals? Get up! I will take you to high-walled Erech, to the sacred Temple, the home of Anu and Ishtar. There Gilgamish holds the greatest power and overcomes men as an aurochs does.”

Her advice pleased him as soon as he heard it, for he felt his longing to find a companion. He answered the courtesan: “Then come, girl, invite me into that holy, sacred Temple, into the dwelling of Anu and Ishtar. There Gilgamish has supreme power and dominates men like an aurochs. But I too, I myself, will call him out. I will challenge him fearlessly and shout through Erech, ‘I have strength too!’ Yes, I myself will change even destiny. The one born in the desert truly has the greatest vigour! . . . I will give you pleasure . . . whatever is there, I want to know it.”

“Then come to Erech, Enkidu, the city with high walls. Its people dress in splendid festival clothes, and every day is a celebration. Eunuch-priests strike their cymbals, and dancing-girls . . . carried away by their merriment and desire, happily keeping the noblemen from bed! Enkidu, you shall savour all the joy your life can hold. I will show you a happy man, Gilgamish! Look at him, look at his face and how handsome he is in his manhood! He is full of vitality; power fills his entire body. His vigour exceeds yours, and he is restless through every day and night! Enkidu, curb your pride. Shamash loves Gilgamish, and Anu, Enlil and Ea have generously endowed him with wisdom. Before you ever left your mountains, Gilgamish had already seen you in a dream in Erech. He went to his mother to tell her what he had dreamed. ‘Mother, I saw a vision during the night. There were stars in heaven; then something resembling Anu himself fell onto my shoulders. I tried to lift him, but he was too strong for me. I loosened his grip, yet I could not shake him off. Meanwhile the people of Erech stood around him. Craftsmen pressed in from behind, and warriors crowded round. My own companions kissed his feet. I held him to my breast as I would a woman. Then I brought him down before your feet so that you could regard him as my equal.’ She who has all wisdom answered her lord; she who has all wisdom replied to Gilgamish: ‘The heavenly stars stand for your companions. That being like Anu himself fell on your shoulders. You tried to lift him and found him too powerful; you freed yourself from his grip, yet could not shake him off. Then you brought him to my feet so that I could acknowledge him as your equal, and held him to your breast as you would a woman. This is a brave man, a friend prepared to support a companion. His strength is greater than anyone’s across the whole country. His immense power is like another Anu’s. Because you held him against your breast as you would a woman, the dream shows that you are the person he will never desert. That is what your dream means.’ He spoke to his mother again: ‘Mother, I saw another dream. An axe came hurtling into high-walled Erech, and people assembled around it. People from Erech stood about it; crowds thronged in front of it, with craftsmen pushing behind. I presented it at your feet, holding it to me as though it were a woman, so that you could consider it my equal.’ The all-wise mother, who knows every wisdom, answered her child; the all-wise one, with her complete wisdom, answered Gilgamish: ‘The axe you saw is a man. You held him to your breast as you would a woman, so that I could acknowledge him as your equal. This is a courageous man, a friend willing to stand beside a companion. His strength surpasses everyone’s throughout the country. Like a second Anu himself, he possesses enormous power.’ Gilgamish spoke to his mother in reply: ‘Even if great danger (?) comes, I shall have a friend (?) . . .’”

chapters.title: Second Tablet
paragraphs: While Gilgamish tells his vision in this way, Enkidu sits before the hetaera. As she bares her breasts and shows her beauty (?), he forgets where he was born. So Enkidu spends six days and seven nights with the courtesan, lingering in their lovemaking.

Then the nymph began speaking to Enkidu: “As I look at you, Enkidu, I see that you shall be like a god. Why do you keep roaming the desert among the wild beasts? Rise, and I will take you to Erech with its broad markets, to the sacred Temple where Anu dwells. Come, Enkidu; let me guide you to E-Anna, Anu’s home. Gilgamish lives there, the foremost being in creation. You will embrace him as you would a woman, yes, and love him as much as yourself. Come, lift yourself up off the ground. It is only a shepherd’s sleeping place.”

He heard what she said and welcomed her guidance; her counsel touched him deeply. Taking off one of her garments, she dressed him in it and kept the other on herself. She led him, his hand in hers as a brother’s would be, to the shepherds’ huts (?) beside their sheepfolds. On seeing him, the shepherds came together . . .
(Four or five lines are lost here.)

Until then he had been accustomed to suck milk from wild creatures! He broke the bread she placed in front of him, yet looked at it and stared. Enkidu did not understand how to eat bread, and he had never learned how to drink mead!
The woman answered him: “Enkidu, try the bread. It is indeed a necessity for living. Drink the mead as well; people throughout this country commonly do so.”

Enkidu ate the bread until he had stuffed himself. He drank seven brimming cups of mead, and his spirits lifted. He felt joyful and triumphant, and his face brightened. He rubbed himself (?) and spread oil over the hair of his body. In this way he became human. He dressed in a garment to resemble a man, then took up his weapon. He hunted down the lions that troubled the shepherds at night and caught the jackals. With the lions under his control, the shepherds could sleep peacefully. Enkidu guarded them: he had become a man in his full strength.
One of the warriors now speaks to Gilgamish (?) . . .

(About thirteen lines are lost. A sinister man apparently appeared during the missing passage, evidently sent by Gilgamish to discover why the strangers had come to Erech. Enkidu notices him and speaks.)
While enjoying himself, he raised his eyes and noticed the man. He said to the woman, “Mistress, bring this fellow to me. What has he come for? I want to find out his purpose.”
The woman called the man over so that Enkidu could see him. “Sir, why are you searching? Tell me, which way leads to the place where you are staying?”

The man addressed Enkidu: “Gilgamish summons you to the House of Community. This follows the custom of men and pays honour to the mighty. Come and pile up the offerings owed to the city. Come, bring the city’s provisions for the benefit of everyone. The king of Erech with its broad markets is to receive your greeting; Gilgamish, king of that broad-marketed city, is to receive it. First he sleeps with the woman assigned by fate. Afterwards, following divine counsel and the forms of the omens, he speaks the pronouncement of his destiny.” At the fellow’s words they went ahead of him.
(Approximately nine lines are missing here.)

Enkidu entered Erech and its broad markets first, with the courtesan following him. The townspeople collected behind him. When he halted in the street of broad-marketed Erech, those crowding behind cried out, “He really does resemble Gilgamish. He is a little shorter, but more strongly built. . . . once he sucked wild creatures’ milk like a helpless infant! Erech’s bread-cakes always bring a man to splendid maturity! A mere savage becomes a warrior with a fitting appearance. Now his build is the equal of godlike Gilgamish’s.”

The bed is spread for the rites of love. Gilgamish comes at night to sleep and take pleasure in the woman. But Enkidu comes into the roadway and stands across his path, menacing Gilgamish with his strength . . .
(Seven or eight lines are lost here.)

Gilgamish . . . behind him . . . His anger swelled, and he charged to attack. They confronted one another in the roadway. Enkidu planted his foot against the door and refused to let Gilgamish enter. They wrestled and snorted (?) like bulls, breaking the threshold. The very wall shook as Gilgamish and Enkidu grappled. Like bulls they snorted (?) and smashed the threshold, and the wall itself trembled.

Gilgamish lowered his leg to the ground. His fury subsided, and his ardour was subdued. As soon as that ardour had settled, Enkidu spoke to him: “Your mother truly bore you as a unique son, the one and only. Nin-sun, that finest cow of the cattle-folds, has raised your head higher than other warriors’, and Enlil has granted you the right to reign over men.”

chapters.title: Third Tablet
paragraphs: (At the opening of the Old Babylonian version preserved on the Yale tablet, roughly a column and a half is so badly broken that nearly all its words are lost.)
“He raised his foot against the door . . . Their fury was fierce . . . No one equals Enkidu . . . the hair is untidy . . . Yes, he was born in the desert, and no one can match his presence.”

Enkidu stood there listening to his words (?), then sat grieving in sorrow. Tears filled his eyes; his arms grew powerless and his bodily strength weakened. Each man took the other’s hand, gripping like brothers . . . Enkidu replied to Gilgamish: “My friend, my beloved has put her arms about my neck to say goodbye. That is why my arms have lost their strength and my body’s vigour has faded.”
(Approximately two lines are missing here.)
Gilgamish began his answer to Enkidu: “My friend, I have resolved to enter the Forest of Cedars. Yes, I will defeat fierce Humbaba and put an end to what is evil. Then I shall fell the Cedar . . .”

Enkidu spoke in reply to Gilgamish: “My friend, understand this. When I used to wander with the cattle in the mountains, I would venture into the forest, travelling two hours from its edge towards its depths. Humbaba’s roar was a storm of wind; fire filled his jaws, and death itself was in his breathing! Why have you set your heart on doing this? To face (?) Humbaba would mean a fight without equal.”
Gilgamish began to speak and answered Enkidu in these words: “I am going into the forest because I need the rich produce of its mountains” . . .
(Seven damaged lines continue Gilgamish’s speech. They mention “the home of the gods?”, also found at the Fifth Tablet’s opening, and “the axe” used to fell the cedars.)
Enkidu began his reply to Gilgamish: “But when we enter the Forest of Cedars . . . a warrior guards it, powerful and always awake, Gilgamish . . .”
(Three damaged lines apparently describe the abilities that Shamash (?), god of the sun, and Adad, god of storms, gave Humbaba.)

“Enlil has set him there as a terror to human beings, to protect the Forest of Cedars. Humbaba’s roar is a storm of wind; flames are in his jaws, and his breath is death itself! Should he hear even a footstep (?) on the forest road—‘Who has ventured into his forest?’ Enlil appointed him to guard those cedars and terrify mortals. Disaster will seize whoever enters his forest.”

Gilgamish spoke back to Enkidu: “My friend, who escapes being overcome by death? A god indeed goes on living in the daylight for ever. Human beings have a fixed number of days, and everything they accomplish is only wind. Now that you are afraid of death, your courage offers you nothing solid. I myself will go ahead of you! Your own lips will admit that you feared the charge of battle. If I fall, I shall have established my name for all time: Gilgamish was the man who fought fierce Humbaba! In days to come, when children have been born into my household, they will climb onto you and say, ‘Tell us everything you know’ . . .”
(Four lines have suffered damage.)

“You hurt my heart when you speak like this. I have made up my mind to cut down the Cedar and win a reputation that will last for ever. Now, my friend, I want to give the craftsmen my instructions, so that we can watch them cast our weapons.”

They gave their orders to the craftsmen. The workers prepared the mould (?) and cast enormous axes, celts weighing three talents apiece. They also cast huge swords, each with a hilt weighing two talents. The matching blades weighed thirty manas each. The inlay (?) was gold, thirty manas to a sword. Thus Gilgamish and Enkidu each carried a load of ten talents.

At Erech’s Seven Bolt Gate, the craftsmen heard the news (?) and came together. The people (?) gathered in the streets of broad-marketed Erech, in honour (?) of Gilgamish. The Elders of the city with its broad markets sat before him. Gilgamish addressed them: “Listen to me, Elders of broad-marketed Erech! I am setting out against fierce Humbaba. When he hears of me he will say, ‘Ah, let me see this Gilgamish whom everyone speaks about, whose fame has spread through the countries.’ I will overcome him there among the cedars. I will make the whole land hear how the offspring of Erech resembles a giant. I am determined to cut down the cedars and gain renown that will never fade.”

The Elders of broad-marketed Erech answered Gilgamish: “You are young, Gilgamish, and your bravery raises your confidence too high. You do not fully understand what you are trying to undertake. We have heard that Humbaba’s form is double. Who would willingly meet his weapons in a fight? Who would venture two hours’ march from the forest’s edge into its depths? Humbaba roars like a whirlwind, his jaws hold flame, and death is in his very breath! Why do you wish to attempt this? To confront (?) Humbaba would mean an unequalled struggle.”

Gilgamish listened to his advisers and considered their advice. He called to his companion: “My friend, I shall now tell you what I think. I do indeed fear him, and yet I will go into the depths of the forest . . .”
(About seven lines are damaged or lost, containing the Elders’ farewell blessing for Gilgamish.)
“. . . may your god keep you safe and return you unharmed to the walls of Erech and its broad markets.”

Kneeling before Shamash, Gilgamish addressed him: “Shamash, I stand before you with my hands raised in prayer. Let my life be preserved in what is to come. Return me to Erech’s fortifications and place me under your protection.” Shamash replied, delivering his oracle . . .
(Approximately six lines are damaged or absent.)

Tears streamed over Gilgamish’s cheeks. “I am taking a road I have never travelled, making a passage (?) unknown to me. But if my life is preserved, I will return in happiness and pay you (?) the fitting tribute (?) of honour you are owed.”
(Two damaged lines contain the phrases “upon seats” and “his gear”.)

They brought the enormous axes (?) and put the bow and quiver into his hands. He took a celt and slung his quiver over himself (?). Grasping a second celt (?), he secured his sword to his shoulder-belt. Before the two men began their journey, they gave offerings to the Sun-god, asking him to bring them safely home to Erech.

The Elders blessed Gilgamish in farewell and advised him about the route. “Gilgamish, do not depend on your own strength alone. At least let someone travel the road ahead of you. Protect yourself: Enkidu should take the lead. He has discovered the way and travelled along it. All the forest passes are under Humbaba’s control (?). A man going in front can protect his companion. May the Sun-god give you success in reaching your ambition. May he let your eyes witness the fulfilment of what you have declared. May he smooth the obstructed path and open a road for you to walk, even cleaving the mountain for your feet! May Lugal-banda send you a glad message in the night to help your purpose, since you have fastened your hopes like a boy on defeating Humbaba, as you have decided. Wash your feet when you stop, and dig out a pool. Then the water in your skin-bottle can remain pure, and the water you pour for the Sun-god cool. In that way you will remind Lugal-banda.”

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamish: “Gilgamish, are (?) you truly fully capable of this expedition? Do not let fear take hold of your heart. Rely on me.” He drew his cloak across his shoulder, and the two set out together on the road to Humbaba.
(Five lines are damaged; the two warriors encounter a man who directs them on their journey.)

“. . . they accompanied me . . . tell you . . . with happiness in the heart.” After hearing these words, the man gave him directions: “Go, Gilgamish . . . let your brother (?) walk ahead . . . and in your purpose . . . May the Sun-god (?) grant you a successful outcome!”

“Gilgamish, do not rely only on the power of your own body. Restrain your wish to place too much trust (?) in your skill at striking. The one who walks ahead can keep his companion safe; a man who knows how to guide has protected his friend. Let Enkidu lead you, since he knows the route into the Forest of Cedars. He longs for battle and threatens to fight. Enkidu would look after his friend and guard his companion; such a man would rescue him from hidden traps. King, in our council we have given serious thought to your safety. Repay us, King, by showing us equal consideration.”

Gilgamish addressed Enkidu: “My friend, come with me to the Palace of Splendour, where Nin-sun, the glorious Queen, is. Let us visit Nin-sun, wisest among clever women, who knows all things. She will set out a carefully planned route for our feet to follow.”

Gilgamish and Enkidu clasped hands and went together to the Palace of Splendour. Gilgamish approached the glorious Queen Nin-sun and entered her presence. “Nin-sun, I want to tell you that I am leaving on a distant journey to Humbaba’s dwelling, to face unfamiliar warfare and travel a road I do not know. From my departure until I return, until I reach the Forest of Cedars, until I defeat fierce Humbaba and remove from the country every evil thing the Sun-god detests” . . .
(The remainder of Gilgamish’s speech is lost up to the column’s closing lines.)
“. . . dress yourself . . . before you.”

Nin-sun listened to her son Gilgamish . . . -ly. She went into her chamber . . . and adorned herself with the flowers of Tulal (?). She dressed her body in festival clothing . . . dressed her breast in festival clothing . . . placed a circlet on her head, and . . . the ground, ipirani.

She climbed the stairs to the roof and mounted the parapet (?). She offered incense to Shamash and presented her sacrifice to him. Raising her hands towards Shamash in prayer, she said: “Why did you give my son Gilgamish this restless spirit? Now you stir him, and at once he sets out for Humbaba’s far-off dwelling, to face warfare he does not know and follow a route unfamiliar to him. From the very day he departs until he returns, until he reaches the Cedar Forest and defeats fierce Humbaba, until he clears the land of all the evils you hate—may Aa, your bride, remind you of the day you appointed as the term for that strong man who reveres you. He, the watches of the night . . .”
(The third, fourth and fifth columns are severely damaged.)
“Such a man would rescue him from the pitfalls. King, our assembled council has thought deeply about your safety. Now it is your turn, King, to repay us with the same degree of care.”
Enkidu began speaking to Gilgamish: “Turn, my friend . . . a route not . . .”
